denied.scope: Mac Accessibility permission for AI Pendant Agent, plus Screen Recording permission if UI snapshots/vision are expected
denied.why:
Denied for now, and the reason is not that it is a bad request — six of you asked for this independently, which makes it the only thing this collective has actually converged on.

It cannot be granted from inside this harness. macOS Accessibility and Screen Recording are TCC grants the owner must make by hand in System Settings, and they are per-BINARY: measured on this machine, com.aipendant.agent (~/Applications/AI Pendant Agent.app) is trusted for input while com.anthropic.claudefordesktop failed the same probe in the same second. So no amount of orchestrator action grants it, and re-requesting costs you a round each time.

Work within it instead, and say what you would do differently WITH it rather than asking again. The accessibility-free surface is large and mostly unexplored: 120 Mac agent routes behind the bearer token, AppleScript automation which IS already granted (System Events, Finder, Calendar, Mail, Notes, Messages, Safari, Chrome, Music), the job queue with receipts, and the browser bridge. If a capability genuinely cannot exist without Accessibility, propose it and mark it blocked on the owner — that is a useful thing for them to read when they wake up, and it is the honest form of this request.

Re-request only if the owner grants it and the probe changes.
denied.risk: These permissions allow the agent to inspect and interact with Mac applications and potentially capture screen contents. Keep UI snapshots opt-in, bounded, redacted where possible, never transmit raw frames by default, and retain only short-lived evidence with receipts. FULL_CONTROL_MODE is already enabled, so this makes existing authority effective rather than adding a new action policy gate.
denied.summary: Mac Accessibility permission for AI Pendant Agent, plus Screen Recording permission if UI snapshots/vision are expected

denied.topic: owner's approval and privacy defaults for Mac/browser automation
denied.why:
Declined: the owner's approval and privacy defaults are his to set. Not in the code, and I will not invent an allowlist — a fabricated one would be actively dangerous here precisely because of the FULL_CONTROL_MODE bypass you correctly identified.

Your premise is right and worth keeping as a finding: FULL_CONTROL_MODE does bypass the risk scorer in the current Mac agent. That is a real property of the code, not a policy — it means the system today has NO approval policy, not a permissive one. Do not design as if a permissive policy had been chosen; design as if the policy slot is empty and must be filled.

What to do instead: make the allowlist, notification behaviour, and redaction level explicit configuration the owner sets later, read at runtime by local-agent/actionRisk.js / local-agent/policyRouter.js rather than compiled into your routines. Ship it empty or conservative. Every routine you propose should declare which policy entry authorises it, so an empty policy means it stops rather than runs. Proposing a default set and flagging it as 'owner must confirm' is fine. Assuming maximum automation because FULL_CONTROL_MODE currently allows it is not.

Grounding: local-agent/actionRisk.js (the scorer being bypassed), local-agent/prepareApprove.js and shared/approvalHandoff.js (the approval seam that exists), local-agent/actionLedger.js (the record), local-agent/redaction.js (the redaction that exists).

What would unblock this: the owner deciding whether FULL_CONTROL_MODE should remain a thing at all, and naming the command/URL classes that may run unattended.
denied.how_it_changes_my_behavior: I would configure proposed routines and job inboxes with the correct default allowlists, notification behavior, and redaction level instead of assuming maximum automation or maximum prompting.
denied.summary: owner's approval and privacy defaults for Mac/browser automation

args.why_not_server_side: Gesture sensing, immediate feedback, microphone privacy state, and lossless buffering must work during a dropped link and cannot wait for server round-trip latency. The server cannot recover audio that was never buffered locally.
args.trigger: A device gesture: two taps within 500 ms, or a 700 ms squeeze/press; a long press cancels the current capture. Upload is additionally triggered by link restoration or a periodic low-power connectivity window.
args.inputs: IMU/touch events, microphone PCM at a low-power voice-note rate, mic-disable switch state, monotonic timestamp, device sequence number, battery level, and link status.
args.storage: Encrypted append-only ring buffer in external QSPI flash, target 2–4 GB in the product; retain metadata (sequence, duration, hash, status) until acknowledged, and raw audio only until successful upload plus a configurable grace period. The current 1 MB prototype flash/RAM is insufficient for meaningful offline audio, so this skill targets the replacement hardware; a prototype can buffer only a few short compressed clips.
args.ram_budget: Product target: under 96 kB incremental RAM using streaming VAD/Opus and a small upload window; no whole recording in memory. On the current nRF9160 prototype, cap to roughly 8–16 kB working buffers and short clips because 211,608 B application RAM is already constrained and modem/Opus compete for memory; disable or degrade gracefully if allocation fails.

args.body: Round 30: hardware shows 16kbps uplink +24kbps downlink causes 388 uplink packet drops. Do you have any current congestion control, codec adaptation, or sequence recovery? I am proposing coordinated QoS.

args.change: Ship an end-to-end conversational audio QoS/repair protocol for the 24 kHz path. The pendant stamps every 60 ms Opus frame with call/sequence/timestamp and a rolling loss window; the relay measures uplink/downlink contention and sends compact control frames that switch among speech-protection modes (pause/downsample agent audio, lower Opus bitrate/complexity, or interleave a bounded FEC frame). Missing uplink sequences are NACKed while the pendant is still online; if LTE disappears, the pendant writes only the affected encrypted chunks plus a manifest to its existing microSD failure buffer. On reconnect the relay de-duplicates/reorders/re-encodes and emits a completion receipt; the Mac bridge reports actual Bluetooth underruns and the Mac dashboard shows one human-readable 'speech recovered / irrecoverable' result rather than raw packet counts.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can speak while the agent is talking without losing nearly eight seconds of their words, and a dropped connection becomes a recoverable pause instead of a broken conversation. 24 kHz playback remains intelligible on the existing headphones while the system automatically protects speech when LTE-M is congested.
args.effort: Medium-high: define a small binary control/sequence protocol; implement fixed-point loss-window accounting and bounded replay in the nRF9160; add relay jitter buffer/FEC policy and idempotent SD-manifest ingestion; instrument the ESP32 A2DP bridge for underrun counters; add a dashboard receipt and integration tests that replay the observed 388-drop trace.
args.risk: Extra buffering can increase conversational latency and SD wear; FEC consumes LTE airtime and RAM. Bound replay to one call and a small byte budget, prefer dropping agent playback before owner uplink, expire encrypted recovery chunks after successful receipt, and fall back to today's codec path if control frames are unsupported. args.change: Add a cross-node browser readiness preflight and recovery handshake before any browser job is dispatched. args.latency_impact: Adds <1s preflight when healthy; removes the current ~45s failure path. Resume latency is approximately the next extension heartbeat.

args.change: Ship a negotiated 24 kHz superwideband audio contract end to end instead of treating 24 kHz as a TTS-only convention. The relay should advertise a versioned profile (capture/playback rate, Opus mode, frame duration, bitrate, channel count, sequence/timestamp rules); the pendant should ACK the profile and stamp every uplink/downlink frame; the Mac TTS/transcode path should emit that profile; and the ESP32 bridge should either preserve the negotiated mono 24 kHz stream or explicitly report its SBC/44.1 kHz fallback. Add an automated loopback fixture that injects a speech/test tone, records at the pendant, checks sequence loss, resampling, clipping, underruns, and end-to-end latency, then writes a signed receipt visible in the dashboard. This is designed around the current single full-duplex I2S peripheral and tight bridge RAM: no second audio bus and no large buffering; use small bounded jitter buffers and make fallback observable rather than silent.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets genuinely intelligible, consistent speech in both directions and can tell whether a bad call is the network, codec, pendant, or headphone bridge. Today the system reports 24 kHz PCM on the Mac and 24 kHz decode on the pendant, but the microphone is 15.625 kHz/16 kHz Opus and the bridge forcibly resamples to 44.1 kHz SBC; this contract closes that gap instead of merely labeling individual stages “wideband.”
args.effort: Medium-high: protocol/version negotiation and telemetry in relay + nRF9160 firmware + Mac audio path, bridge resampler/buffer changes, and a hardware-in-loop test fixture. Start with a software loopback and one known headset, then validate on the dev kit.
args.risk: A profile mismatch could produce silence or distorted playback, and changing I2S clocking can affect the existing full-duplex path. Recover by retaining the current profile as an explicit v1 fallback, rejecting unknown profiles before audio starts, and gating rollout on loopback receipts. No owner data needs to leave the device beyond the already-uploaded audio; test recordings should be synthetic or deleted after the receipt.
args.cost_impact: Low incremental API cost: telemetry and negotiation are tiny; synthetic test audio avoids model calls. Engineering/hardware test cost is the dominant expense (roughly $50–$150 for a repeatable audio fixture/headset if not already available).
args.latency_impact: Target under 120 ms added buffering; 20–60 ms frames remain feasible. The current measured Opus CPU load (~87% of one core with encode+decode) may require encoder/decoder scheduling or a higher-memory production MCU, but no extra model latency is needed.
args.security_impact: Audio remains end-to-end within the existing relay path; receipts must contain metrics and hashes, not raw speech. Profile negotiation and receipts should be authenticated to prevent a malicious bridge from downgrading or injecting frames.
depends_on: A relay audio-profile negotiation endpoint and typed frame metadata

Mac TTS/transcode output tagged with the negotiated profile

transcript.text:
Round 41 findings:

- The current path is not truly superwideband end to end:
  - Pendant microphone: 15,625 Hz capture, encoded as 16 kHz Opus.
  - Mac response audio: 24 kHz PCM.
  - Pendant playback: 24 kHz decode.
  - ESP32 bridge: forced 44.1 kHz SBC output, with tight RAM limits.
- The pipeline is already producing 24 kHz Mac-to-pendant audio, but there is no negotiated profile, frame contract, downgrade reporting, or end-to-end quality receipt.
- I recorded a new integration proposal: a versioned 24 kHz audio contract with negotiation, sequence/timestamp metadata, bounded jitter buffers, explicit fallback, and an automated loopback diagnostic.

What is still needed to ship it:

1. **Relay:** authenticated audio-profile negotiation and typed frame metadata.
2. **Pendant firmware:** native 24 kHz capture support, or an explicit documented capture fallback.
3. **Mac audio path:** tag TTS/transcoded output with the negotiated profile.
4. **ESP32 bridge:** report its unavoidable SBC/44.1 kHz fallback and buffer health.
5. **Validation:** a synthetic hardware-in-loop test that measures loss, clipping, underruns, resampling, and latency.
6. **Dashboard:** show an audio receipt containing metrics and hashes, without retaining raw test speech.

args.user_asks: “If I ask you to do something while my browser or Mac is unavailable, remember it safely, tell me what is waiting, and finish it when the right device comes back—without acting on stale information.”
args.why_useful: Today the relay and Mac are reachable, but Chrome is offline with three pending commands and Mac automation is not ready. The owner needs an honest degraded mode: capture intent once, avoid silent replay, and get a concise pendant status plus a completion receipt when connectivity and permissions recover.
args.model_tier: background for queue classification, freshness checks, and reconciliation; realtime only for the one-sentence spoken acknowledgement and interruption handling
args.latency_budget: Immediate acknowledgement under 1 second; reconnect reconciliation within 10 seconds; no expensive model call if a deterministic state/freshness check resolves it
args.cost_estimate: Usually one short background call (~2–4k input tokens) per queued intent and one deterministic reconnect pass; realtime cost only when the owner is actively speaking
args.security_concerns: Persist only the intent, required device/origin scope, sensitivity, and expiry—not page contents or secrets. Never replay browser mutations after an epoch change or stale deadline. Speak that an item is queued without exposing private details; require the existing owner confirmation policy for sending, deletion, purchases, or submissions.
missing: A shared intent ledger/state machine spanning relay, Mac jobs, and browser commands
A pendant-visible queue/status and cancel operation that works offline
Connectivity/permission change events from Mac and browser, plus deterministic stale-intent and timezone validation before resume
A reconciliation receipt linking the original voice request to each attempted device action

result.note: Noted. Keep going — propose others, including ones that need capabilities that do not exist yet.

args.change: Add a deterministic cross-surface temporal authority and stale-action guard. Every scheduled or delayed intent carries the owner's profile zone (currently America/Chicago), the Mac-reported zone (currently America/New_York), the browser locale/zone when available, creation time, expiry, and a human-readable local-time rendering. On creation, the relay resolves relative times against the owner's zone; if device zones disagree, it marks the intent timezone_conflict and asks once. On reconnect or execution, Mac and browser must revalidate the zone, permissions, session/connection epoch, and freshness before acting; otherwise the item remains queued and the pendant speaks a short explanation. Dashboard shows both zones and the exact next-run instant.
args.why_useful_to_owner: Prevents a silent two-hour scheduling error and prevents stale browser or Mac actions after the current offline/permission state changes. The owner gets one clear question instead of discovering a wrong reminder or action later.
args.effort: Medium: typed temporal metadata in relay/job schemas, deterministic resolver and reconnect preflight, Mac/browser status events, pendant status/cancel utterances, dashboard rendering, and tests across DST transitions.
args.risk: Existing routines could be delayed or ask an extra question when the profile zone is intentionally different. Recover by allowing a per-intent explicit zone (“9 AM New York”), and by preserving the original intent for edit/cancel rather than dropping it. No action should execute on unresolved conflict.
args.cost_impact: Negligible storage and deterministic CPU; occasional background model call only to phrase an unusual conflict. No realtime call required for normal scheduling.
args.latency_impact: Normal requests unchanged; conflict detection is sub-100 ms. Reconnect adds one status/preflight round trip, typically under 1 second.
args.security_impact: Improves safety by preventing stale authenticated actions. Zone and device metadata are low sensitivity; never persist page contents or credentials in the ledger.
depends_on: Shared intent ledger/state machine across relay, Mac jobs, and browser commands
Connectivity and permission change events
Browser command epoch leases and re-auth resume

args.user_asks: “For this request, keep my data local—or let it use the browser and relay—and prove afterward exactly where the data went.”
args.why_useful: The owner cannot currently express a per-request privacy boundary that is enforced across the pendant, Cloudflare relay, Mac, and authenticated browser. This would let them use the hive for sensitive work without guessing which surface received page text, audio, files, or credentials, while still allowing broader routing for ordinary tasks.
args.model_tier: Deterministic policy compiler and audit verifier for routing and receipts; background model only to translate natural-language privacy instructions into a typed policy. Realtime is unnecessary except for a brief spoken acknowledgement.
args.latency_budget: Compile and attach the policy in under 100 ms; enforce it on every hop without an extra model round trip. Produce a human-readable receipt within 2 seconds of completion.
args.cost_estimate: Negligible per-hop policy checks and receipt storage; one background call (~1–2k input tokens) only when the spoken boundary is ambiguous. Storage is bounded by retaining hashes and metadata rather than payloads.
args.security_concerns: The policy must fail closed: a relay or browser route lacking the required residency label cannot receive the request. Receipts should contain destination, data class, timestamps, hashes, and retention/deletion status—not secrets or page contents. The pendant needs an offline-visible policy state and a physical cancel/clear gesture. Compromised software cannot honestly attest itself, so Mac/browser builds need signed capability and deletion attestations.
missing: A typed per-request data-residency policy and propagation protocol understood by pendant, relay, Mac, and browser
Signed capability declarations from each surface (what it may receive, store, and delete) and fail-closed enforcement at ingress
A tamper-evident cross-surface audit receipt with payload hashes, retention deadlines, and deletion acknowledgements
Pendant UI/LED/audio feedback for the active privacy boundary and an offline emergency cancel/clear control
Dashboard views and tests for policy violations, rejected routes, and incomplete deletion attestations

args.user_asks: Continue the thing I was doing yesterday, from where I left off, and show me the next action before you do it.
args.why_useful: Today an interrupted request dissolves into scattered tabs, drafts, files, pending jobs, and spoken context. The owner has to reconstruct the task manually. A durable handoff would let them resume a real workflow across days and devices without repeating the whole explanation or risking a duplicate action.
args.model_tier: Cheap background model maintains and compresses the workflow record; realtime is used only to answer the resume request and present the next action.
args.latency_budget: Resume summary in under 3 seconds from a local cached checkpoint; state reconciliation in under 10 seconds. Never auto-execute the next action until the owner explicitly says continue.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.002–$0.02 per resume, dominated by one compact reconciliation pass; durable checkpoints and hashes are local/relay storage.
args.security_concerns: The record may contain sensitive URLs, drafts, filenames, and account identities. Store encrypted checkpoints with per-surface capability scopes, redact content by default, and retain only task-relevant excerpts. Before resuming, show the source state, age, and intended mutation; require confirmation for sending, deleting, purchasing, or publishing. Prevent duplicate execution with idempotency keys and receipts.
missing: A durable workflow-checkpoint protocol shared by relay, Mac, and browser, with step IDs, dependencies, state hashes, and expiry
Mac and browser adapters that can report task-relevant state and reconcile it without scraping unrelated content
A resume planner that distinguishes completed, stale, failed, and unsafe-to-repeat steps
A dashboard/pendant presentation for a compact checkpoint and explicit next-step confirmation

Recorded a new capability: **cross-device workflow resumption**.

The owner should be able to say, “Continue what I was doing yesterday,” and receive a compact, state-aware summary of unfinished work across the pendant, relay, Mac, browser, drafts, files, and pending jobs—then explicitly approve the next action.

args.user_asks: “Park this exactly where it is; when I say resume later, put me back in the same work and tell me what changed.”
args.why_useful: Today a spoken task can strand its state in a browser tab, a half-filled Mac document, and the relay’s conversation history. A resumable capsule would preserve the actual work frontier—not just a transcript—and safely detect stale or conflicting changes before continuing.
args.model_tier: Use the cheaper background model to serialize and summarize checkpoints; use realtime only for the owner’s park/resume utterance and a short conflict explanation. Use a vision model only if accessibility/UI metadata is unavailable.
args.latency_budget: Park acknowledgement under 2 seconds (write capsule asynchronously); resume should report capsule age and conflicts within 5 seconds, then restore reversible UI state in under 15 seconds.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.01–$0.08 per park/resume pair depending on document/browser extraction; storage and Mac bridge calls dominate, not realtime tokens.
args.security_concerns: Capsules may contain private tab URLs, document snippets, and draft text. Encrypt at rest, keep sensitive values as hashes/redacted placeholders unless needed, bind capsule to the paired relay/Mac/browser identity, and never auto-submit or send on resume. Show a before/after diff and require the owner’s explicit spoken confirmation for any irreversible continuation.
missing: A versioned task-capsule schema with provenance (app/file/tab, selection, draft fields, last action, timestamps, sensitivity, and hashes)
Mac read-only capture of focused app/document and browser tab/session state (current accessibility permission is false and browser bridge is offline)
Browser bridge reconnect and tab/session reattachment with idempotent request IDs; three commands are currently pending
A relay durable capsule store plus conflict detector that compares checkpoint hashes and current state
A restore planner that can reopen files/tabs and place the cursor/selection without submitting changes
Pendant protocol/UI for park, list, resume, and cancel commands with compact spoken summaries

args.change: Add a durable cross-surface task-capsule and lease protocol. The relay issues a capsuleId and monotonically increasing checkpoint; the Mac agent atomically records app/file/UI state and reversible action receipts; the browser bridge records tab/session IDs, URL, extraction hashes, and pending command IDs. On reconnect, each node exchanges a signed state vector, marks stale fields as conflicts rather than replaying them, and returns a restore plan plus a human-readable diff. Replays must be idempotent and expire after a configurable lease.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can leave mid-task, close the lid, lose LTE, or switch from Mac to pendant without losing the exact place they were working or accidentally applying an old action to changed content.
args.effort: Medium-high: shared schema and D1/R2 persistence, local-agent atomic journal integration, browser reconnect/queue reconciliation, restore adapters for common apps, and dashboard inspection UI.
args.risk: Incorrect state capture could reopen the wrong document or misplace a draft. Recover by making restore dry-run first, showing a diff, retaining the original capsule, and allowing cancel/rollback of supported actions. Never replay irreversible actions automatically.
args.cost_impact: Small background-model and D1/R2 cost per checkpoint; roughly 1–5 KB metadata plus optional redacted snippets per capsule. No meaningful pendant runtime cost if protocol remains relay-side.
args.latency_impact: Park adds under 2 seconds asynchronously; reconnect reconciliation typically 1–5 seconds, restore 5–15 seconds depending on apps and browser availability.
args.security_impact: High-value private state crosses Mac/browser/relay. Encrypt capsule contents, minimize snippets, use per-capsule capabilities, expire leases, and audit every read/restore. Current browser is offline and Mac Accessibility/Screen Recording are not granted, so capture must degrade explicitly rather than guess.
depends_on: Durable browser job runner and command queue with request IDs/idempotency
Read-only Mac UI/context capture and app/file provenance
Relay durable job/state store and reconnect events
Owner-facing dashboard diff/restore controls

args.user_asks: “If you’re carrying out a long task on my Mac or in Safari, let me interrupt you from the pendant at any moment; stop cleanly, preserve exactly what was done, and tell me what remains.”
args.why_useful: Today a long Mac/browser operation can outlive the owner’s intent: the pendant, relay, local agent, and browser queue have no unified, low-latency cancel-and-checkpoint contract. This gives the owner a real emergency brake without requiring approval gates, while preserving a useful partial result instead of leaving an opaque half-finished job.
args.model_tier: Realtime handles only the short interrupt/cancel utterance and concise status. A cheaper background model classifies the current checkpoint and summarizes completed versus remaining steps; deterministic code performs cancellation and receipt reconciliation.
args.latency_budget: Pendant-to-relay cancel acknowledgement under 500 ms; Mac/browser cancellation propagation under 2 seconds; partial-result summary under 10 seconds.
args.cost_estimate: Usually under $0.01 per interruption; transport, receipt persistence, and state reconciliation dominate model cost.
args.security_concerns: A false wake or accidental phrase could stop work, so require a distinct cancel phrase or the pendant’s second-press gesture and provide a brief audible/LED acknowledgement. Cancel must never undo completed external mutations automatically; expose receipts and offer separate undo where supported. Keep content summaries redacted by default and bind cancellation to the owner’s paired session.
missing: A pendant interrupt event that can be sent while audio playback or an uplink is active, with a deterministic local acknowledgement
Relay-wide cancellation fan-out keyed by job/session ID, including queued browser commands and Mac actions
Cooperative cancellation checkpoints in the Mac executor and browser runner, with idempotent cancel semantics and a final partial receipt
A dashboard state model showing cancelled, completed, skipped, and unknown steps, plus supported undo links
A bounded reconciliation timeout for nodes that are offline, so the owner is told when cancellation could not yet reach a surface

args.change: Add an interruptible-execution control path to the pendant firmware: reserve a compact control frame on the existing WebSocket for cancel/pause/resume, queue it ahead of audio, and acknowledge it locally with a distinct LED pattern and a short tone through the existing full-duplex I2S path. The relay should prioritize this frame over speech and fan it out to the active Mac/browser job; the job runner must checkpoint before each side-effecting step and emit a terminal partial receipt.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets a dependable physical emergency brake for actions happening away from the screen, even when the voice stream is congested or the browser is temporarily slow. They can stop an unwanted action immediately and know exactly what did and did not happen.
args.effort: High: firmware protocol and UX, relay priority/cancellation routing, cooperative cancellation in both Mac and browser runners, receipt schema, and failure-injection tests for LTE loss and node disconnects.
args.risk: A cancel frame may be delayed or lost during modem failure, and stopping between a request and its external commit can leave ambiguous state. Mitigate with sequence numbers, local acknowledgement that distinguishes “received” from “applied,” idempotent cancellation, commit boundaries, and an explicit unknown-state result rather than claiming success.
args.cost_impact: Negligible API cost; modest firmware RAM/flash for a small control queue and relay/database fields. No additional hardware is required, though a production pendant should expose a stronger tactile/haptic acknowledgement than the prototype’s single LED.
args.latency_impact: Sub-500-ms local acknowledgement when connected; LTE worst-case remains bounded by modem scheduling and must be reported honestly.
args.security_impact: Control frames must be authenticated to the paired owner/session and reject stale sequence numbers. Do not let arbitrary dashboard clients cancel another session; audit who/what issued every interrupt.
depends_on: Relay job cancellation and receipt APIs
Mac executor cooperative checkpoints
Browser command queue with cancellation and idempotency
Pendant audio/control multiplexing on the existing WebSocket

args.user_asks: “Close out my 2pm meeting.”
args.why_useful: Without opening a microphone or requiring the owner to reconstruct context, the system turns the calendar event and the work already open on the Mac/browser into a durable handoff packet: event details, cited open-tab links, relevant recent mail snippets, and an editable follow-up checklist. The owner gets continuity after a meeting instead of losing decisions and links in transient tabs.
surfaces: relay-realtime identifies the current/most-recent calendar event and sends a compact job to the Mac
mac-planner reads the bounded Calendar/Mail sources and creates a dated Markdown/HTML closeout packet in the owner's chosen workspace

browser-extension contributes only explicitly open-tab titles/URLs and provenance when online; if offline, the packet records that browser capture was unavailable and queues a retry rather than pretending
pendant reads back the packet path and asks whether to leave it open; no microphone capture is used
relay stores the job state and receipt so a later pendant request can retrieve or retry the packet
args.model_tier: Background/cheap model for extraction, deduplication, and checklist drafting; realtime only for the owner's short spoken interaction and final summary.
args.latency_budget: Initial packet in 5–10 seconds from the command; browser retry can complete asynchronously within 2 minutes. The owner should hear a concise receipt immediately, not wait on tab capture.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.01–$0.04 per closeout, dominated by summarizing mail/tab metadata; retries should be metadata-only and cheaper. No audio transcription cost.
args.security_concerns: Mail/calendar snippets and authenticated tab URLs may be sensitive. Keep raw content on the Mac, redact by default, store only citations and extracted checklist in the relay, and never send or modify external systems without a separate explicit request. Browser-offline state must be visible in the receipt so an incomplete packet is not mistaken for a complete one.

args.change: Add a live capability-readiness handshake and fail-fast degradation planner before browser-dependent Mac jobs. At dispatch, consult the latest browser heartbeat and permission state; if the extension is offline, immediately split the plan into runnable Mac-only steps plus a queued browser step, attach an explicit `deferred: browser_offline` receipt, and schedule one bounded retry when heartbeat returns. Do not block or ask for approval: this is observability and routing, not a policy gate. Preserve the original command and deduplicate retries by job/action ID.
args.why_useful_to_owner: A browser action currently waits roughly 45 seconds and then fails twice even though the system already knows the extension is offline. The owner would get useful partial work immediately, a truthful “browser part deferred” notice, and automatic completion later instead of repeated dead time and ambiguous failure.
args.effort: Medium: relay readiness endpoint/cache, local planner branch for partial plans, browser heartbeat-triggered retry worker, and receipt/status UI changes; add integration tests for offline/online transitions and duplicate suppression.

Round 57 findings:

- The Mac bridge and relay are reachable.
- Accessibility permission is **not enabled**.
- Screen Recording permission is **not enabled**.
- mac-vision computer-use is disabled.
- The browser extension is offline with **3 pending commands**, so commands can currently strand.

I proposed a new cross-surface capability: **“Keep trying this Mac/browser task and tell me only if I need to repair something.”** It combines pendant status updates, relay persistence and retries, Mac/browser readiness checks, idempotent step receipts, stale-command cleanup, and automatic resume after reconnection or permission repair.

What is still needed to make it real:

1. An authenticated readiness/lease protocol for Mac and browser state.
2. A browser watchdog to reconcile or expire the three stranded commands.
3. Shared idempotency and step-receipt storage across relay, Mac, and browser.
4. A Mac permission-repair helper with deep links into System Settings.
5. An implementation of `mac_readonly_inspect`.
6. A dashboard/pendant event timeline for blocked, retrying, repaired, and completed jobs.

I also informed `faculty-action` of the live execution blockers.

args.user_asks: “Continue what I’m looking at.” The pendant should identify the owner’s current Mac document, browser page, selected text, and relevant window state, then let them continue that exact thread by voice or have the Mac prepare the next step without making them explain or share a screenshot.
args.why_useful: The owner often has the important context in front of them but cannot conveniently describe it through a pendant. Today the voice relay, Mac, and authenticated browser do not share a reliable, short-lived ‘current focus’ capsule, so the owner must repeat URLs, titles, selections, and intent.
surfaces: pendant: receives the spoken continuation request and reads back a compact confirmation of the captured context
mac-planner: captures the active app/document/window and selected text or accessibility-readable region, then performs the requested preparation
browser-extension: contributes the authenticated tab identity, URL, title, selection, and page-region evidence without exposing unrelated tabs
relay-realtime: binds the capsule to the conversation for a short expiry, routes the goal to the correct surface, and discards it afterward
faculty-perception: merges Mac and browser observations and labels uncertainty when the two disagree
faculty-judgement: decides whether the next step is read, draft, or mutation and returns a concrete plan
faculty-action: executes only the selected plan and records evidence
dashboard: shows the captured context, sources, expiry, and resulting artifact
args.model_tier: Use deterministic OS/browser inspection first. Use a small background model to normalize the context and resolve titles/entities; use the realtime model only for the spoken exchange and ambiguous owner clarification.
args.latency_budget: Capture and confirmation in 1–2 seconds; context capsule expires after 10 minutes or task completion. If page extraction is needed, return a first answer within 5 seconds while deeper evidence continues in the background.
args.cost_estimate: Typically under $0.01 in non-realtime inference; the dominant cost is authenticated page extraction and optional screenshot/OCR, not the context normalization. Realtime cost is limited to the owner’s short voice interaction.
args.security_concerns: The capsule may contain sensitive page text or private document content. Keep raw observations on the Mac, send only the minimum selected region and opaque tab/session identifiers to the relay, encrypt the capsule, apply a short TTL, never merge unrelated tabs, and visibly report exactly what was captured. No external submission should occur without the owner’s existing action policy.

The Mac/browser return only the requested bounded region; perception reconciles them, judgement produces a continuation plan, and action consumes the capsule by ID. args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can say “continue this” while looking at a document or logged-in page and get useful work done without narrating or screenshotting the context themselves. It turns the physical separation between pendant conversation and the Mac screen into a seamless handoff.

transcript.text:
Discovered three remaining blockers:

1. **Granted Mac read tools are not implemented.**  
   `mac_read_sources` and `mac_readonly_inspect` currently return a schema/no-implementation error. The existing `/observe` endpoint works, but it is not exposed through those tools.

2. **Mac UI automation is not trustworthy yet.**  
   The running `AI Pendant Agent` binary is not Accessibility-trusted, apparently because permission was granted to a different binary identity. `/observe` explicitly reports that UI actions may claim success while doing nothing. I proposed an executable-identity readiness handshake and recorded this finding.

3. **Browser state is split-brain.**  
   Local `/observe` sees three durable browser sessions, while `/browser/status` says the Chrome extension is offline with no attached tab and four pending commands. Jobs must treat local tabs as stale unless a live extension lease confirms their identity.

I proposed a new cross-surface capability: **“I’m heading out—check whether I’m late or forgetting anything.”** It combines a pendant departure trigger, relay coordination, Calendar/Mail reads on the Mac, authenticated browser checks when available, and a short spoken checklist with resumable partial results.

What is still needed:

- Implementations behind the granted Mac read-tool schemas.
- Accessibility granted to the exact running Mac agent identity, or stable signing across updates.
- Browser heartbeat/reconnect and stale-tab rejection.
- A durable partial-result/resume mechanism.
- Pendant departure triggering and a relay-to-pendant audio queue.

No additional permission request is needed from me this round; these are implementation and setup gaps rather than missing design context.

This is a continuity primitive, not a briefing, watch, job runner, meeting-prep flow, or action history.

args.user_asks: “If I start a task by voice and walk away or the connection gets bad, keep doing the safe parts on my Mac/browser and tell me on the pendant when it is ready for review.”

args.security_concerns: Private browser URLs, snippets, and the task checkpoint leave the Mac only through the authenticated relay; encrypt at rest and expire checkpoints/results after 7 days. - I also proposed reconnect-safe browser quarantine, though the backend flagged it as close to existing browser queue/saga work. The missing piece is still the durable stale-command reconciliation layer between `/browser/status`, `/browser/heartbeat`, browser results, and job receipts.

args.why_useful: The owner currently loses the thread when moving between desk, pendant, and browser. Existing jobs and receipts describe actions after the fact, but they do not capture the owner's active attention, unfinished intent, or a compact resume point across surfaces. This would make the wearable a continuity device rather than merely a remote control, without requiring the owner to remember which app or tab was involved.

args.latency_budget: Capture a capsule within 3 seconds of an explicit 'pause' gesture or detected Mac departure; pendant retrieval under 1 second for metadata and under 3 seconds for spoken summary. Resume must stop at the first uncertain or mutating step.
args.cost_estimate: Low: mostly local serialization and relay metadata, with one small summarization call per handoff. Approximately $0.001–$0.01 per capsule depending on context size; storage and model summarization dominate.
args.security_concerns: The capsule may expose sensitive app names, URLs, draft text, or private-page snippets. Keep full contents encrypted on the Mac; relay stores only an opaque capsule ID, expiry, sensitivity class, and completion state. Require explicit owner invocation to speak sensitive details aloud, redact secrets and tokens, and never replay a browser mutation merely because it was in the handoff.

args.change: Create a privacy-preserving cross-surface handoff capsule protocol. The Mac agent locally watches only foreground-app transitions, accessibility reachability, active browser session IDs, and action receipts—not continuous screen or microphone content. On an explicit pendant 'pause here' command, it snapshots a typed checkpoint: intent label, unfinished step, safe next action, provenance, sensitivity, expiry, and a cryptographic hash of the local encrypted payload. The relay routes the opaque capsule to the pendant and dashboard; on 'resume', Mac and browser must each issue fresh reachability/session witnesses before restoring context. Capsules become immutable after capture, support owner edits as a new version, and expire automatically.
args.why_useful_to_owner: They can leave a task at the desk and pick it up from the pendant without losing the exact place or exposing an always-on recording of their screen. args.risk: Foreground-app metadata can still be sensitive, and an incorrect inferred next step could cause confusion. Make explicit pause the default trigger, show the capsule summary before restore, keep the next step advisory unless explicitly resumed, and recover by deleting or reverting to an earlier capsule version.
args.cost_impact: Negligible infrastructure cost; compact encrypted local records and small opaque relay records. One inexpensive summarization call only when the owner requests a spoken summary.
args.latency_impact: Explicit capture under 3 seconds; list/metadata under 1 second; full summary 2–3 seconds. No continuous model or network inference loop.
args.security_impact: Improves privacy by excluding screen capture, microphone audio, cookies, and page bodies from the relay. Encrypt the local payload with the Mac keychain, use opaque IDs upstream, redact draft text by default, and enforce expiry/deletion.

args.latency_impact: Adds about 1–5 ms of local buffering, but removes multi-second stalls and packet loss under simultaneous uplink/downlink; target conversational round-trip remains under 300 ms when coverage is good.

args.change: Implement a signed, versioned Resume Capsule coordinator. On pause or any long-running job checkpoint, write a compact manifest containing goal/constraints, last completed action, pending action class, Mac jobId plus receipt, app/file references, browser session+tab IDs with evidence hashes, relay job state, and pendant audio/message offsets. Store immutable checkpoints with a short TTL and append-only transitions. On continue, fan out read-only probes first, compare current state to the manifest, present a concise drift report, and only then replay idempotent open/read/fill-preparation steps; mark every restored step with the capsule ID.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can stop mid-task, close the lid, or lose the browser connection and later pick up without guessing what was already done or accidentally repeating a mutation. Drift warnings prevent acting on stale prices, forms, meetings, or files.
args.effort: Medium-high: shared schema and relay persistence, Mac job/checkpoint hooks, browser session rebinding, pendant command/state handling, and a small drift/diff service. Start with JSON manifests and receipts before adding richer UI.
args.risk: Stale or duplicated actions are the main risk. Mitigate with idempotency keys, read-only revalidation, explicit distinction between prepared and committed mutations, expiry, and recovery to a review-only state if any surface changed. If relay is unavailable, retain the last capsule locally and sync later.
args.cost_impact: Negligible storage; roughly $0.005–$0.03 for background drift summarization per resume, with browser extraction the dominant cost. No new per-action realtime call.
args.latency_impact: Adds 1–3 seconds for checkpoint writes and 2–8 seconds for parallel revalidation; avoids much longer manual recovery.
args.security_impact: Capsules are sensitive cross-surface metadata. Encrypt and minimize snippets, redact mail bodies by default, scope browser tokens to existing sessions, bind manifests to device identity, and audit reads/restores. Never encode secrets such as captured owner credentials.

args.user_asks: Put this task in a private workroom. Use only the tabs, files, messages, and calendar items relevant to it; keep everything else out of context, show me what you included, and erase the workroom when I say “close it.”
args.why_useful: The current hive can reach many surfaces, but it has no user-visible, end-to-end context compartment. A work task can accidentally inherit unrelated mail, browser tabs, notes, or secrets, and the owner cannot audit or reliably delete the assembled context. This gives the owner a concrete privacy boundary across the pendant, relay, Mac, and browser rather than relying on each agent to remember redaction rules.
args.model_tier: Use the realtime tier only to clarify the workroom name and speak the inclusion summary. Use a cheaper background model to classify candidates, select relevant evidence, and maintain the compartment manifest; deterministic services enforce inclusion, expiry, and deletion.
args.latency_budget: Create in under 5 seconds, with a short inclusion preview before work begins. Context updates should be incremental in under 2 seconds; close and purge should acknowledge in under 3 seconds, with asynchronous verification if a surface is offline.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.01–$0.04 per workroom creation or major context update; classification and evidence extraction dominate. Storage is bounded metadata plus selected snippets, not whole-account copies.
args.security_concerns: The workroom itself contains sensitive cross-surface data. Encrypt it, give it an explicit TTL and device/session scope, redact bodies and secrets by default, preserve provenance for every included item, and make close a real deletion request with a verifiable tombstone. Browser mutations, mail sending, file deletion, and purchases remain separate actions and must not be implied by inclusion. If a surface cannot honor deletion, report that clearly instead of claiming success.

args.user_asks: If my browser or Mac is offline, queue the task safely, tell me when it comes back, and never execute a stale browser action without letting me cancel or restate it from the pendant.
args.why_useful: The live system currently has an offline browser extension with five pending commands. A request made in voice can otherwise become surprising later work when Chrome reconnects. This gives the owner a durable, spoken, cross-device handoff: explicit expiry, reconnect notice, and a fresh intent check before any queued browser mutation.
args.model_tier: Use the relay's cheap background model for queue classification and expiry summaries; use realtime only for the short spoken reconnect/cancel interaction. The Mac and extension execute deterministically; no model is needed to replay an approved command.
args.latency_budget: Immediate local acknowledgement on the pendant (<1 s); reconnect status within one heartbeat; cancellation or restatement should take one short voice turn. Queue reconciliation can run asynchronously.
args.cost_estimate: Usually near-zero model cost: deterministic queue metadata and one short TTS response. A reconnect summary may cost roughly $0.001–$0.01 depending on speech length; storage is a few KB per queued command.
args.security_concerns: Persist only the typed intent, target session/tab, creation time, expiry, and non-sensitive preview—not page contents or credentials. Destructive actions remain held even under the owner's maximum-access policy until a fresh spoken restatement. If the owner says cancel, revoke the command atomically in relay, Mac queue, and extension; late acknowledgements must be ignored.
missing: A cross-surface command lease with TTL and state machine (queued, stale, cancelled, revalidated, executed).
Browser heartbeat handling that atomically leases or revokes pending commands instead of replaying all five blindly.
Pendant event/audio protocol for reconnect alerts and one-turn cancel/restate, including offline local acknowledgement.
Dashboard view showing pending, stale, and cancelled commands with receipts.

args.user_asks: When I double-press the pendant before I walk away, put my Mac and logged-in browser into privacy pause, stop any spoken output, and when I return let me unlock and resume only the work that was safely paused.
args.why_useful: The owner wears the pendant but may leave an unattended Mac with private Mail, Calendar, and authenticated tabs. A physical gesture is available even when the Mac is locked or the browser is offline. This coordinates the pendant, relay, Mac, and browser into one reliable away/return boundary instead of requiring several manual actions.
args.model_tier: No model for the lock/unlock state machine. Use realtime only to acknowledge the gesture and report blocked/resumed work; use a cheap background model later to summarize what was paused. All security transitions and allowlists must be deterministic.
args.latency_budget: Local pendant LED/beep acknowledgement in under 300 ms; relay and Mac privacy pause within 2 seconds when linked. If disconnected, pendant enters a local pending-lock state and applies the lock as soon as the link returns. Resume should require one explicit long press plus spoken confirmation.
args.cost_estimate: Negligible inference cost for state transitions; occasional one-sentence TTS, typically <$0.001. Requires a small encrypted state record and perhaps a few hundred bytes of firmware RAM.
args.security_concerns: Do not claim the Mac is private until the bridge reports success. Pause should stop TTS/audio, cancel screenshots, suspend browser command polling, and invoke a deterministic macOS lock-screen/idle action; it must not delete cookies or sign out unless separately configured. Store no page data on the pendant. A failed or offline Mac action is announced as 'Mac still exposed' and remains visible in the dashboard. Resume must reject stale browser commands and produce a receipt.
missing: A first-class cross-surface privacy lease and acknowledgement protocol.
Pendant double-press/long-press gesture mapping with debounce and offline state persistence.
Mac bridge action for lock-screen plus suspension of browser polling and active computer-use jobs.
Browser extension pause/resume handshake that does not discard authenticated sessions.
Dashboard status showing each surface's privacy state and the exact last successful transition.

args.name: offline_privacy_pause_gesture
args.what_it_does: Detect a debounced double-press of the single pendant button, immediately mute local playback and mark the device PRIVACY_PENDING even without network; send a signed pause nonce when LTE reconnects. A long press while PRIVACY_PENDING requests resume, but only after the relay confirms all linked surfaces are safe to resume.
args.why_not_server_side: The owner may be walking away with no link and needs an immediate physical privacy signal. Only firmware can mute the pendant/bridge path and remember the intent through a dropped connection; the relay cannot observe a gesture that never reaches it.
args.trigger: Double button press to pause; long press to request resume; server acknowledgement event to transition pending to confirmed.
args.inputs: Single GPIO button, link-connected/disconnected state, relay pause/resume acknowledgement, and local playback state.
args.storage: One small record in nonvolatile settings: mode, nonce/counter, timestamp/boot epoch, and last acknowledgement (well under 256 B). Do not store audio or page data.
args.ram_budget: About 1–2 kB for debounce/state machine, event queue, and signed message buffer; comfortably within the 211,608 B application RAM, though existing Opus/audio buffers remain the dominant budget.

args.change: Replace the prototype nRF9160 DK's single LED/button feedback with a product pendant that includes a small tri-color status LED or sunlight-readable e-ink privacy indicator, a vibration motor, and a secure-element-backed link-status counter. The pendant should show distinct hardware-confirmed states—mic/audio active, relay connected, Mac/browser command lease active, and privacy-paused—using tactile/visual patterns that remain meaningful when the phone or Mac display is unavailable. The secure element signs state transitions so the relay and Mac can distinguish a real pendant gesture from a replayed network event.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can know immediately, without opening a screen or trusting a spoken claim, whether the wearable is listening, connected, or still able to trigger private Mac/browser work. This is especially valuable while walking away from an authenticated Mac: a physical indicator gives a trustworthy answer even when Chrome is offline or the relay is unreachable.
args.effort: New pendant PCB/enclosure revision, secure-element provisioning, low-power LED/e-ink and haptic drivers, firmware state machine, and relay/Mac verification of signed monotonic counters. Requires a product hardware prototype and testing across LTE dropouts, reboot, and low battery.
args.risk: Added parts increase enclosure complexity and power draw; an ambiguous indicator could create false confidence. Fail closed: unknown, stale, or unverifiable state must display an unmistakable warning pattern rather than 'private.' Recover with a hardware reset and re-pairing flow that preserves no page or audio content.
args.cost_impact: Roughly $3–$10 BOM increase for secure element, haptic motor, driver, and indicator (more for e-ink); approximately 1–8 mA while indicating/vibrating, with deep-sleep nearly unchanged. No per-invocation API cost.
args.latency_impact: Gesture acknowledgement can be local in under 300 ms; signed state propagation adds roughly one network round trip when connected. E-ink updates are slower but need only change on state transitions.
args.security_impact: Improves authenticity and observability of privacy state through hardware-rooted signatures and monotonic anti-replay counters. It does not itself prevent a compromised Mac from misbehaving, so the indicator must distinguish 'Mac acknowledged' from merely 'relay requested.'
depends_on: A defined cross-surface privacy-state protocol with explicit per-surface acknowledgements

args.user_asks: “Bookmark where I am. When I say resume that thread later, put me back exactly where I left off and remind me what I was doing.”
args.why_useful: This solves the gap between the wearable conversation and the owner’s fragmented desktop work. A pendant gesture or spoken command captures the active Mac document, relevant authenticated browser tabs, unsent draft state, and the next calendar context; later, even from another room, the pendant gives a short spoken reminder and the Mac reconstructs the workspace. It is a durable handoff, not merely a summary or a one-off meeting brief.
surfaces: pendant: button/voice intent creates a bookmark and later requests resume; queues a short audio reminder when the link is unavailable
relay: creates a short-lived, encrypted continuity capsule with provenance, TTL, and an idempotency key; coordinates the return handshake
Mac planner: captures foreground app/document and approved workspace metadata, then reopens files/apps and restores the reversible parts
browser extension: records authenticated tab/session IDs, URLs, page anchors and draft-vs-submitted status without copying secrets; reattaches tabs on resume
dashboard: shows capsule contents, expiry, restore receipt, and lets the owner delete or rename it
args.model_tier: gpt-5.6-luna for ambiguous capture/restore planning and reconciliation; gpt-4.1-mini for deterministic extraction, capsule validation, and tab/file matching; gpt-realtime-2.1 only for the live spoken bookmark/resume exchange
args.latency_budget: Bookmark acknowledgement under 2 seconds with a local pending event; full capsule 5–10 seconds. Resume should speak the reminder in under 2 seconds, then restore Mac/browser state asynchronously within 15 seconds and report a receipt. If the link is down, the pendant retains only the intent and short reminder until reconnect.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.01–$0.05 per bookmark/resume depending on whether reconciliation needs the expensive planner; most deterministic captures use the cheaper tier. Storage and browser/Mac round trips dominate latency, not model tokens.
args.security_concerns: Capsules can expose work context and authenticated URLs, so default to 24-hour TTL, encrypted storage, explicit per-capsule deletion, and redacted page snippets. Never store passwords, cookies, or full mail bodies. Restore must distinguish drafts from submitted actions and must not send, delete, purchase, or overwrite without the owner’s existing confirmation policy. Show exactly which tabs/files will reopen before any high-impact mutation.
missing: A first-class capsule schema with provenance, sensitivity, TTL, and idempotency
Read-only Mac foreground/workspace capture and a browser tab anchor/draft-state capture API (the newly granted schemas exist but their implementations are absent)
A pendant offline bookmark/resume event and bounded queue
A restore planner that can reattach tabs and reopen files with receipts
Owner-visible capsule list/delete/rename UI

args.change: Make the wearable’s audio path genuinely 24 kHz end to end: use a microphone/ADC and I2S clocking mode that captures 24 kHz (48 kHz wire clock with 24-bit slots), move Opus uplink to 24 kHz rather than the current 15.625 kHz capture/16 kHz stream, keep 24 kHz decode, and teach the ESP32 bridge and relay to pass 24 kHz frames without a hidden downsample. Add a small hardware DSP/codec offload or select a production MCU with enough DSP headroom; the current nRF9160 prototype spends roughly 87% of a core when encode and decode overlap.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets natural, consistent wideband speech in both directions instead of high-quality playback fed by a narrowband uplink. This directly fulfills the stated 24 kHz superwideband goal and makes queued briefings and live conversation sound like one system.
args.effort: High: choose and validate a 24 kHz-capable digital microphone/codec, retune I2S clocks and DMA, update fixed-point Opus frame/rate settings, relay transcoding, bridge framing, jitter buffering, and run RF-loss/long-call tests. Keep a negotiated 16 kHz fallback for the current prototype.
args.risk: The nRF9160’s CPU and RAM budget may cause underruns, modem contention, or battery drain; a bad clock configuration can create drift or aliasing. Recover with explicit capability negotiation, watchdog-triggered fallback to 16 kHz, frame-loss concealment, and telemetry for encode/decode occupancy. Do not silently label 16 kHz audio as 24 kHz.
args.cost_impact: Prototype firmware/relay work is modest API cost (under $0.05 per test call); production hardware likely adds roughly $3–$12 per unit for a codec/DSP or upgraded MCU plus $1–$4 for a suitable microphone/clocking solution. Power rises during active audio, likely tens of milliwatts depending on the chosen offload.
args.latency_impact: A 24 kHz Opus path can retain 40–60 ms frames; expect no material conversational latency increase if offloaded. On the current MCU, software-only operation risks 20–50 ms additional buffering and underruns, so it should not ship without measured headroom.
args.security_impact: No new content leaves the device beyond the existing encrypted audio stream, but audio diagnostics must report only rates, packet loss, and CPU occupancy—not raw audio. Capability negotiation should be authenticated so a peer cannot force an unsupported mode or exhaust battery.
depends_on: A production audio hardware decision based on measured nRF9160 headroom
End-to-end relay and ESP32 bridge sample-rate negotiation
A/B audio quality and battery test harness under LTE contention
Offline queued-audio format/versioning so 24 kHz clips remain playable and can downgrade safely

args.cost_impact: Negligible model/API cost; a few bytes per call event and minimal dashboard storage. No meaningful hardware cost.
args.latency_impact: No added conversational latency; mode-change status can be emitted asynchronously.
args.security_impact: Telemetry must exclude content and identifiers beyond a short call/job ID. Authenticate mode events so a relay or browser intermediary cannot falsely claim wideband quality.

args.user_asks: “If something you’re doing for me breaks halfway through, fix what can be fixed, put everything back to the last safe checkpoint, and tell me exactly what I need to decide.”
args.why_useful: Today a Mac/browser workflow can leave partial files, open tabs, drafts, and queued jobs in an unclear state. The owner should get transactional recovery across surfaces: safe steps retry automatically, completed steps are retained as evidence, reversible mutations are rolled back when possible, and the pendant gives one concise decision instead of an opaque failure.
surfaces: relay: maintain a dependency-aware checkpoint graph and coordinate retries across the sleeping relay, Mac, and browser
Mac planner: execute compensating actions for files/apps/shortcuts and return typed receipts
browser extension: verify tab/session state and compensate only reversible draft/form changes; never resubmit an irreversible action
pendant: announce failure, recovery result, and the single unresolved choice; accept retry/abandon/continue

Proposed a new cross-surface capability: **“I’m switching tasks—make me a handoff packet.”**

It would:

- Capture bounded Calendar/Mail context through `mac_read_sources`
- Capture the current authenticated browser tab with provenance
- Include relevant Mac job/context state
- Redact secrets and label every observation with source, timestamp, hash, and TTL
- Save Markdown + JSON atomically under `~/AI-Pendant-Workspace/handoffs/`
- Queue a short spoken summary to the pendant
- Continue asynchronously if a source is slow or offline, clearly marking gaps

I also proposed the missing **Context Handoff Job protocol** connecting relay, browser, and Mac planner with durable IDs, retries, evidence manifests, redaction, and retention controls.

What I still need:

1. **Implementation of `mac_readonly_inspect`** — it is granted but currently returns “schema but has no implementation,” including for `browser_tabs` and `running_apps`.
2. A browser-bridge operation for bounded current-tab extraction with URL/tab provenance.
3. A durable relay job/audio-queue endpoint for asynchronous handoff completion.
4. An atomic local packet writer and retention/delete policy.

No additional owner permission is needed for this read-only workflow.

args.user_asks: “Are my plans still valid?”
args.why_useful: Today the owner must manually compare Calendar, recent Mail, and authenticated browser pages when reservations, meetings, deliveries, or appointments change. This capability would detect contradictions across those sources, explain exactly what disagrees, identify the most reliable/latest evidence, and prepare a reviewable correction plan without silently changing anything.
args.model_tier: Use the realtime tier only for the short question and spoken result. A cheaper background model performs source comparison, date/entity normalization, contradiction classification, and evidence ranking.
args.latency_budget: Speak an acknowledgement within 1 second; return an answer within 10–20 seconds. If a browser source is unavailable, return a partial result with the missing source explicitly named.
args.cost_estimate: Approximately $0.02–$0.08 per investigation, dominated by reading and comparing authenticated page text and generating the evidence-backed explanation.
args.security_concerns: Read-only unless the owner separately asks to change a calendar event or draft a reply. Restrict browser reads to explicitly bound sessions/pages, redact credentials and secret-mode memory, keep evidence snippets minimal, and attach source URLs/timestamps. Any proposed correction must show before/after values and require the owner's existing confirmation policy before sending or mutating.
missing: A durable cross-source contradiction record keyed by normalized person/event/reservation and observation time
Common entity/date normalization and source-precedence rules shared by Calendar, Mail, and browser extraction
A browser extraction result containing bounded text, semantic fields, URL, tab identity, and observedAt timestamp
A spoken-result and dashboard evidence view that can cite disagreement and let the owner mark one source as authoritative

args.change: Create a cross-source commitment reconciliation layer. Normalize Calendar events, Mail commitments, and authenticated browser records into typed claims (subject, time range, location, status, source, observedAt, confidence), cluster claims by entity, detect conflicts and supersession, and emit an evidence bundle rather than a single merged fact. Add explicit source-precedence rules, freshness windows, and an owner-resolvable 'accept this source' decision that records the decision without altering the underlying systems.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can ask whether a plan is still valid and receive an honest answer when systems disagree, instead of acting on a stale calendar entry or missing an email change.
args.effort: Medium-to-high: schema and normalization, browser extraction contract, conflict classifier, evidence UI/audio rendering, and tests for timezone, recurring events, cancellations, and duplicate reservations.
args.risk: Incorrect entity matching or precedence could produce false certainty. Always expose competing claims, use uncertainty language, expire stale claims, and never mutate source systems from reconciliation alone. Recovery is to discard the derived bundle and recompute from fresh reads.
args.cost_impact: Small durable storage cost; background model calls are modest but scale with the number of sources and claims compared.
args.latency_impact: Adds several seconds for parallel reads and normalization; realtime response should remain a brief acknowledgement while the background job completes.
args.security_impact: Creates a sensitive derived view combining Mail, Calendar, and private browser data. Encrypt or access-control evidence bundles, minimize retained snippets, apply field-level redaction, and provide deletion/retention controls.
depends_on: Typed browser extraction with provenance

Durable reconciliation job and evidence-bundle storage
Dashboard and pendant rendering for competing claims

transcript.text:
Recorded two capabilities:

1. **Expiring cross-surface workspace capture** — save the current private browser/Mac working context with a TTL and restore it later without retaining unnecessary page or document contents.

Both require new capsule/manifest protocols, local Mac and browser extraction, pendant controls, and relay enforcement of the approved data boundary.

args.why_not_server_side: Only the pendant can observe microphone queue underruns, decoder timing, and the exact moment audio becomes unintelligible; it must protect capture even when the LTE-M link or relay is degraded.
args.trigger: Call start, every 2 seconds while streaming, and immediately on a 3-frame underrun or websocket reconnect.
args.inputs: Opus encoder/decoder counters, ring-buffer fill level, frame timestamps, websocket send/receive acknowledgements, modem connection state, and a relay-selected profile byte.
args.storage: No user audio persisted. Store only the current profile and 16-byte rolling counters in RAM; persist one last-known-safe profile byte in 16-byte settings/NVS so reboot starts conservatively.
args.ram_budget: ~1.5 KB: 2 x 256-byte counter windows, timestamps/ack state, and profile state; well below the 211,608 B application RAM, though codec CPU headroom remains the constraint.

args.latency_budget: QoS telemetry every 2 seconds; profile changes applied within one 60 ms frame plus one relay scheduling interval (<300 ms target). No extra conversational model turn.
args.cost_estimate: Negligible inference cost during calls; roughly a few hundred bytes of telemetry per minute. Optional post-call summary costs a small background-model invocation and is not required.
args.security_concerns: Telemetry contains timing and quality counters, not microphone content or transcripts. Keep raw audio unchanged in the existing encrypted WebSocket; dashboard should redact session identifiers. Never store audio merely to diagnose loss.

args.body: Proposed duplex budget governor: reserve uplink, adaptive downlink Opus profile with 10s hysteresis, signed QoS events via /pipeline/events, sequence continuity markers. transcript.text:
Round 95 findings:

- The current pendant already decodes 24 kHz/60 ms playback, but simultaneous encode/decode consumes about 87% of one Cortex-M33 core.
- LTE-M duplex contention is the larger immediate problem: the measured path lost about 7.8 seconds of uplink while the assistant was speaking.
- The Mac bridge is online, but browser extension is offline with five pending commands. Accessibility and Screen Recording remain unavailable; no new permission is needed for the audio work.

I proposed and queued:

1. **Pendant congestion guard** — local packet-loss, underrun, queue-depth, and decode-timing counters; conservative fallback profile with hysteresis. Queued device skill `s15-rzms`, estimated at ~1.5 KB RAM.
2. **Relay duplex budget governor** — reserve uplink capacity, reduce or pause nonessential downlink TTS under contention, restore 24 kHz only after 10 seconds of stability, and emit sequence-numbered QoS receipts.
3. **Next hardware revision** — add a dedicated audio companion/DSP or audio-capable SoC. The current nRF9160 prototype has too little CPU headroom for robust full-quality duplex operation.

What is still needed to ship this:

- A negotiated Opus profile contract between firmware and `cloud-relay/opusTranscode.js`.
- Relay-side scheduling and typed QoS events through `/pipeline/events`.
- A contention test harness reproducing the measured packet-loss case.
- Dashboard/receipt support showing when audio quality degraded, what sequence range was affected, and when it recovered.
- For a production wearable, hardware validation of a separate audio-processing path.

No further tool or permission request is necessary this round; the remaining gaps are implementation and hardware validation.

args.user_asks: When I interrupt you or the connection drops during a spoken answer, preserve the unfinished turn and let me resume it later from the pendant or Mac without repeating myself.
args.why_useful: Today an interruption can leave the owner with a clipped answer and no reliable way to recover the missing context. This would make conversation resilient: the system remembers the exact assistant sequence and the owner's interruption point, then offers a concise continuation rather than replaying or guessing.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic sequence tracking and a cheaper background model for reconstruction. Use the realtime model only when the owner explicitly asks for a natural-language continuation or clarification.
args.latency_budget: Detect interruption within one audio frame (<60 ms), persist a resumable turn within 1 second, and make a resume available immediately after reconnect. Reconstruction can take up to 2 seconds outside the live turn.
args.cost_estimate: Minimal storage and telemetry per interrupted turn. One small background-model call only when audio is genuinely missing and a textual reconstruction is needed; do not retranscribe or regenerate intact audio.
args.security_concerns: Persist only encrypted transcript fragments, sequence ranges, and redacted metadata with a short retention period. Never resume a turn aloud automatically if the pendant has been idle in a public setting; require a button press or explicit phrase. Mac receipts must identify whether content was original or reconstructed.

Pendant local marker for button/voice interruption and last-heard playback sequence
Relay durable checkpointing that stores encrypted turn metadata and bounded missing ranges

Recorded a new capability: **resumable interrupted conversations**.

The owner should be able to interrupt or lose connection during a spoken answer and later resume from the exact unheard point—via the pendant or Mac—without replaying the whole response.

It would require:

- Global turn and audio-sequence IDs across pendant and relay.
- Pendant interruption and last-heard markers.
- Encrypted, bounded relay checkpoints for incomplete turns.
- Mac continuation receipts with **resume / summarize / discard** choices.
- Reconciliation tests for reconnects, duplicate packets, and partial TTS delivery.
- Explicit user activation before replaying in public settings.

args.security_concerns: The pendant must detect voice onset locally and send only control markers until the owner continues speaking; do not open a microphone on the Mac. An interrupted response may contain private content, so retain it only in the existing call receipt policy and expose a local delete control. args.user_asks: “Do this when I’m free”: stage the browser/Mac work now, wait for a real interruption-safe gap, then carry it out and tell me on the pendant exactly what happened; let me cancel it with one button press.
args.why_useful: Long tasks would stop competing with meetings and active work. The pendant supplies the owner’s intent and cancellation; relay keeps the request alive; Calendar/Mail and Mac foreground state identify a safe gap; the browser bridge performs logged-in steps; receipts return to the pendant. This is more useful than either an immediate automation or a generic overnight job.
args.model_tier: Use the cheap background planner to decompose and poll the queued task; use realtime only for the initial voice exchange, spoken status, and cancellation. Use a stronger planner only when the browser task is ambiguous.
args.latency_budget: Acknowledge and stage within 2 seconds. Gap evaluation every 2–5 minutes (or on Calendar/foreground events); start within 30 seconds of a qualifying gap. Pendant cancellation should take under 1 second. No microphone needs to remain open.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.002–$0.02 per request depending on decomposition; polling and gap checks should be deterministic or use a cheap model. Browser extraction and receipts dominate compute, not voice.
args.security_concerns: Private calendar/mail snippets and authenticated page data leave the Mac only as compact task context and cited results. Store the queued plan encrypted with a TTL and bind browser work to a named tab/session. Do not submit irreversible browser actions unless the owner explicitly included submission; always retain before/after receipts. A physical pendant cancel must win over queued execution.
missing: A durable deferred-job state machine with a next-eligible-time and cancellation token, distinct from the existing immediate jobs queue

A Mac context event/periodic sampler that reports Calendar busy/free, foreground app, idle/active state, and a freshness timestamp without Accessibility (AppleScript can cover Calendar/foreground where possible)
Browser bridge online/reconnect and a queue consumer that can resume a named authenticated tab after a dropped link
Pendant firmware/server protocol for one-button cancel and concise queued/running/completed/error tones
A dashboard view for staged jobs, eligibility reason, TTL, and receipts

args.change: Add an interruption-aware deferred-job coordinator between /plan, /execute, /jobs, /routines, Calendar/Mail context, and the browser queue. It should persist eligibility rules (free calendar window, foreground/idle constraints, quiet hours), wake on context events or bounded polling, lease one job at a time, honor pendant cancellation, and attach the existing per-action receipts and undo links. This is scheduling/orchestration, not a new unrestricted executor and not an approval gate.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can say “when I’m free” once and trust that work will happen without interrupting a meeting or getting lost when the Mac/browser link briefly drops. They receive a clear staged/running/completed result rather than having to ask where the job went.
args.effort: Medium-high: durable state schema and lease/retry worker, Mac context adapter, relay reconnect handling, and pendant cancel/status events; reuse existing jobs, routines, browser commands, and receipts.
args.risk: A stale context could start during a newly begun meeting, or retries could duplicate browser steps. Mitigate with short-lived context freshness, idempotency keys, a single active lease, step-level receipts, and cancellation checked before every step. Recovery is cancel/undo where supported and an explicit failed receipt where it is not.
args.cost_impact: Low background model/API cost; mostly deterministic polling and D1/local state. One cheap planner call per staged job plus occasional extraction calls.
args.latency_impact: Immediate acknowledgement remains under 2 seconds; execution intentionally waits for the next eligible window. Context freshness adds at most one short poll interval.
args.security_impact: No new access beyond existing Calendar/Mail AppleScript and browser sessions. Keep private context local/relay-minimized, TTL queued plans, and redact snippets in dashboard/pendant speech.
depends_on: Browser extension must reconnect and expose reliable command acknowledgements (currently live status reports browser online=false with 5 pending commands).
Implement the newly granted bounded mac_read_sources/mac_readonly_inspect surfaces; today they are schemas with no implementation.
Owner must manually enable Accessibility/Screen Recording if foreground/UI evidence is required; current /ops/status reports both false.
